title: Centre releases Rs 1.09 lakh crore to states early for festivals; Bengal gets Rs 7,866 crore
dek: The November instalment of states' share of central taxes, normally due on 10 November, was paid on Thursday to help states spend before the festive season. West Bengal received the fourth-largest amount.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Union government on Thursday released Rs 1,09,019 crore to state governments as their regular monthly share of central taxes, five days ahead of schedule, the Finance Ministry said. West Bengal's share of the instalment is Rs 7,866 crore, the fourth-largest of the 28 states.

The instalment would normally have been paid on 10 November. The ministry said it was brought forward to 5 November because of the coming festive season, and to help states speed up capital spending and pay for their development and welfare programmes.

## Who gets what

Uttar Pradesh receives the largest amount, Rs 19,208 crore, about 17.6% of the total, according to the state-wise table in the ministry's release. Bihar is next with Rs 10,845 crore, then Madhya Pradesh with Rs 8,010 crore and West Bengal with Rs 7,866 crore. Maharashtra gets Rs 7,022 crore and Rajasthan Rs 6,460 crore.

Among Bengal's neighbours, Odisha receives Rs 4,819 crore, Jharkhand Rs 3,660 crore, Assam Rs 3,552 crore and Sikkim Rs 365 crore. The smallest amount goes to Sikkim, followed by Goa with Rs 398 crore.

Bengal's Rs 7,866 crore is about 7.2% of this instalment. The table does not include the Union Territories, which are funded separately.

## How the money is shared

Under the Constitution, the Centre shares a portion of the taxes it collects, called the divisible pool, with the states. A Finance Commission, appointed every five years, decides how large that portion is and how it is split between states, using a formula that gives weight to population, area, income and other factors. Poorer and more populous states such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar receive larger shares. The money is paid in monthly instalments, and the Centre sometimes releases an extra or early instalment ahead of festivals or at the end of the financial year.

The transfers are untied: unlike grants for central schemes, which come with conditions on how they are used, states can spend the money as they choose. For most states, and especially for the poorer ones, the tax share is one of the largest single sources of revenue, alongside their own collections from GST, stamp duty, excise on liquor and taxes on vehicles and fuel.

## Why it matters for Bengal

The early payment comes as Bengal's new government sets out spending plans. On Thursday the state unveiled an industrial policy that promises incentives for investors, including electricity tariff relief and a share of employers' provident fund contributions, as The Declaration reported. Industry bodies in Kolkata welcomed the incentives, reports said. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has also promised to fill government posts, including 7,200 permanent panchayat jobs. Any extra cash in hand before the festival season eases the state's monthly payments, though the instalment is an advance on money the state was due anyway, not an increase in its share.

## What happens next

The next instalment is due in December. Because November's payment has been made early, states will receive no further routine transfer this month. The ministry did not say whether an additional instalment would be released later in the year.
